title: The inside story of Lewis Hamilton’s first F1 test
excerpt:
As Lewis Hamilton gears up for this Sunday's Sao Paulo Grand Prix, he will be preparing to make his 400th Grand Prix start in Formula. To mark the milestone, F1.com revisits his first F1 test with McLaren as fellow Briton Alex Lloyd, who he tested alongside that day, recalls his first-hand account of the outing which kicked off Hamilton’s journey to seven world titles…

It’s December 1, 2004. McLaren have arrived at a cold and crisp Silverstone to give some up-and-coming racers their first drive in an F1 car. Included on the run plan are McLaren Autosport BRDC Award winners in Lloyd and Jamie Green – a victor in Euro Formula 3000 and the champion of that year’s Formula 3 Euro Series respectively.

But there’s another name on the list. McLaren’s long-time protégé Lewis Hamilton, a teenager who lit up the karting scene and was making an impression in single-seaters, having beaten Lloyd to the Formula Renault UK title in 2003 and finished fifth overall as a rookie in the highly competitive F3 Euro Series category won by Mercedes-backed Green.

For all three, it marked the realisation of a dream they had shared since their days in karts, with an added layer to the story for Hamilton and Lloyd, who were rivals on the track but had developed a strong friendship off it.

“Lewis and I were very close,” Lloyd tells F1.com. “We grew up together, we were sort of best friends from age 10 through to 15 or something. We vacationed together and during the summer holidays between school we’d hang out each other’s houses. So, I knew Lewis really well.

“At the McLaren test, we were saying to each other, ‘Can you believe this is happening?’ Going back to our karting days, when we said, ‘One day we’re going to drive an F1 car’, then it’s, ‘Okay, this is the day!’ It was nice that it was both of us at the same time, getting that opportunity to do it and experience it.”

As touched on, it was jumper and scarf weather when Hamilton, Lloyd and Green arrived at the gates of the British Grand Prix venue for their breakthrough test, with the wintry conditions adding to the challenge ahead of them – but it was, thankfully, dry.

Each driver would get two short, solo runs in the McLaren MP4-19 – which did not live up to its title-contending predecessor but still won a race in Kimi Raikkonen’s hands – to tread the fine line of wanting to impress McLaren and keeping the car on the track.

“I don’t know how it is for the award winners today, but it was 10 minutes, another 10 minutes, and that’s it,” Lloyd points out. “It felt very much like a lot of build up for this short moment that you’ve got to try and grasp, even if there’s not really much you can do in 20 minutes.

At the McLaren test, we were saying to each other, ‘Can you believe this is happening?’ It was nice that it was both of us at the same time.Alex Lloyd

“The big thing I remember was thinking, ‘Wow, we got lucky here in December at Silverstone, that it’s still dry’. It meant we could actually experience the car a little bit, because if it’s torrential rain, it’s still cool, but you’re not really going to feel the grip and all those things that you want to experience in an F1 car.”

For Lloyd, who spent some of his youth living near Silverstone and was often awoken by the sound of cars pounding around the circuit, the grunt from a Mercedes V10 engine and the downforce generated from an Adrian Newey-designed car meant his jaw dropped when he left the pits and hit the throttle.

“I think none of us had ever driven anything like it,” Lloyd smiles. “I thought I’d be prepared having driven an F3000 car, which at that point in time was about as much as you could do without getting into an F1 car, but it was a whole different ball game.

“For the first couple of laps, I remember thinking, ‘I don’t know if I can cope with this’, as my brain couldn’t keep track with what was happening. You hit the throttle pedal and you were thrown into the back of the seat. It just felt like a spaceship!

“It took about three laps and then your mind starts to slow down a little bit and you can work out what’s happening. You go from not a panic mode, but sort of, ‘How the hell do I drive this thing?’ It was so ridiculously fast and a much bigger step than I imagined.”

As the laps ticked by, two standout features for Lloyd, Green and Hamilton to get to grips with were super sharp steering and carbon brakes that required careful bedding in before the left pedal delivered its optimal, scarcely believable level of stopping power.

“I remember being shocked at how light the power steering was, because I’d been driving in Euro Formula 3000 with this big, heavy steering, and then suddenly it’s precise,” he says. “The steering felt really awkward, as if you were skating around for the first couple of corners.

“I’d also never driven carbon brakes and damn near crashed at the first turn! I didn’t realise that carbon brakes, until you get heat in them, they don’t work at all. It was like having bicycle brakes on an F1 car for the first corner. I had to swerve around a cone and thought, ‘Oh God’.

“You needed to apply 100 plus pounds of brake pressure to get it to work. The team were showing me data against Juan Pablo Montoya’s, how much force he was putting on the pedal compared to me, and at the beginning I was applying around 25% of it. Then it’s, ‘Okay, I’ve really got to start doing a leg press with this thing!’”

It begs the question: how did all three drivers approach their dream chance with so many elements to learn and so much potential for something to go wrong?

“I remember Lewis going out, running through the gears, cruising for a lap or two, building from a speed perspective,” continues Lloyd. “I think it was probably a little bit the comfort of knowing this was going to be the first of many opportunities. I think he didn’t really have that sort of feeling that he needed to prove himself as such.

“I think Jamie probably did have that feeling. He went out there and you could see it, all guns blazing… I did the same. I think Lewis probably felt a lot more comfortable in his position of, ‘Okay, I can build up to this properly’, the way I probably should have done too. But again, what are you going to prove in 20 minutes?”

Indeed, lap times were not shared with the media after the test, while McLaren’s end-of-day press release made no reference to them, with the team offering a basic summary and quotes from Lloyd and Green about what it felt like to receive their prize runs.

Lloyd did note the presence of some rudimentary timing on the pit wall that then ran from Woodcote to Copse, though, even if the testing trio were out on track at different points in the day and approaching each run in their own way.

Lewis’ dad was there, my dad was there, Jamie’s family was there. You could see everybody there with their stopwatches.Alex Lloyd

“McLaren had very much said, ‘No timing, you will not impress us in 20 minutes. Just enjoy it, drive the car, soak it in, there’s no pressure’,” Lloyd comments. “Nobody was timing officially, but of course, everybody’s parents… Lewis’ dad was there, my dad was there, Jamie’s family was there. You could see everybody there with their stopwatches.

“I remember Lewis and I basically matched times, and I think Jamie was a second or so faster than us – he was on it. But for all three of us, there was probably still a lot of performance left on the table. None of us were on the ragged edge.

“You learn as much as you can in 20 minutes, but you also know that if you had a whole day, you’d be going a lot faster. But it was fun to see us all somewhat battling for a good time, even though it’s completely irrelevant at the end of the day.”

F1's youngest World Champions as Antonelli smashes record

With the test completed, Lloyd, Green and Hamilton came back down to earth and continued their respective motorsport journeys – all aiming to one day turn that brief taste of F1 machinery into something more.

Green was placed in German touring car series DTM by his backers Mercedes for 2005 and stayed there for some 15 years, with an F1 seat never materialising, while Lloyd – struggling to find the necessary finances – made sporadic outings in Italian Formula 3000, Formula Renault 3.5 and A1 Grand Prix before heading to the United States.

As it transpired, Hamilton was the one to make it all the way to the F1 grid, winning the Formula 3 Euro Series and the GP2 title back-to-back to show McLaren that he had what it took to jump in alongside reigning two-time World Champion Fernando Alonso in 2007.

“It was cool to have that experience with Lewis in an F1 car for the first time, and for me to watch from afar in the US and just see his progression,” says Lloyd. “Especially that first year at McLaren when he was coming in and taking on Alonso, and damn nearly winning the championship.

“When Lewis got put into F1, he was ready, he was there. It felt like there really wasn’t much of a learning curve or rookie mistakes… A couple of little things here and there, but in general it was as if he had been prepared perfectly, was dropped into this seat and away he went. Witnessing a few of those steps along the way was nice.”

Childhood friends, Lloyd and Hamilton inevitably lost touch with each other as the years went by, with the former building his new life in the US – which included taking the Indy Pro Series title and reaching IndyCar – and the latter becoming a global superstar.

“We stayed in contact a little bit for a while,” says Lloyd. “When I moved to America, I very much moved to America, I didn’t really come back home… I think we did sort of drift apart. It’s maybe a little easier to keep in contact nowadays with social media.

“I remember I was racing at Indianapolis in the Pro Series in 2007, a race he won in F1, so it was good to catch up with him there. But it became increasingly rare that we were around the same areas, when I was primarily on the American scene, and at that point not really travelling to the UK or Europe at all.”

Now, more than two decades on from that first F1 test, Hamilton is a record-equalling seven-time World Champion with a record number of 105 pole positions and 106 wins to his name.

That success has been achieved across two lengthy stints with McLaren and Mercedes, but he continues to fight at the top racing for Ferrari after one of F1’s biggest ever driver moves.

“It’s kind of crazy that the test was 20 years ago,” Lloyd chuckles. “Now look at where Lewis is… Am I surprised that he’s been very successful in F1 and achieved great things? No, not really. That looked pretty realistic for him. Everybody could see he was extremely talented.

Am I surprised that he’s been very successful in F1 and achieved great things? No, not really. Everybody could see he was extremely talented.Alex Lloyd

Lloyd adds: “But I think what’s been probably more impressive is the way he’s handled himself outside of the track. At that level of fame, that level of notoriety, you tend to see people go one way or the other. I think he’s very much remained humble and doesn’t tend to stoop to those levels that others do when things get a little heated here and there.

“He tends to take that higher road, and I think he’s done a great job of being a role model for younger people coming up. The level of success that he’s had… I don’t know how many people would have done it to that degree. But again, it’s not really a surprise.

“His whole family are genuinely very, very nice people, and humble people who always had to work hard. Especially in those early years, the pre-McLaren years, working to get to where they were. I think all of that shines through in who Lewis is today. It’s pretty damn impressive.”

A version of this article first appeared in December 2024

title: Camara to make F1 debut for Haas in Sao Paulo
excerpt:
Ferrari junior and Formula 2 standings leader Rafael Camara will drive for Haas at the upcoming Sao Paulo Grand Prix, with the team confirming Esteban Ocon will no longer compete for them this year.

Over the Mexico City Grand Prix weekend, Ocon – who previously announced he would be departing Haas at the end of the season – was replaced by reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa.

He finished P10 to score a point in his first race for the team, but pre-existing commitments in the World Endurance Championship this upcoming weekend has opened the door for Camara – who is signed to Haas for 2027 – to make his F1 debut earlier than originally planned at his home event.

The Brazilian has several years of experience in the junior formulae, securing titles in Formula Regional European Championship and Formula 3, but he also impressed in Haas' 2025 challenger during a Testing of Previous Cars (TPC) test in August.

Team Principal Ayao Komatsu said: "We have now notified Esteban Ocon that he will not return to a race seat with TGR Haas F1 Team this season.

"Such decisions are never made lightly, as was the case in Mexico City – but then, as now, we feel this is firmly in the best interests of the team moving forward.

"The conversations that ultimately unfolded between the team and Esteban remain an internal matter, and we will continue to respect the private nature of closed-door situations.

"Looking ahead, we’ve chosen Rafael Camara to drive alongside Ollie Bearman at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix. Having excelled in his TPC outing in August, we know Rafa’s capabilities and we’re looking forward to welcoming him into the team this weekend and working with him through his Formula 1 debut driving the VF-26 in Brazil."

title: The incredible F1 legends' cars that sold at auction
excerpt:
A Honda NSX once owned by three-time World Champion Ayrton Senna has sold for £871,250 (approximately $1,169,000 USD) at auction in London, more than three decades after the Brazilian drove the car during his Formula 1 career.

Senna’s NSX is far from the only road car with an illustrious Formula 1 connection to go under the hammer. From Ferraris, McLarens and more – F1 drivers past and present have owned some extraordinary machinery away from the track.

Here are some of the most eye-catching examples.

Senna’s special Honda

Senna's relationship with Honda began during his time at Lotus in 1987, before he joined the Honda-powered McLaren team the following season and claimed his first World Championship.

We've all seen the famous footage: Senna, white socks and loafers on, working the pedals of the Honda NSX as he attacks Suzuka. But the Brazilian's association with the NSX went much deeper than simply driving one, with the three-time World Champion providing feedback during its development and perhaps becoming the most famous name associated with the NSX.

By the start of 1991, Senna was a two-time World Champion and, under an agreement with Honda, had access to an NSX for his personal use. The red example was registered in Portugal in March that year, stored in Lisbon and delivered to the F1 great whenever he was in the country.

Senna drove the car to that year's Portuguese Grand Prix at Estoril. It later appeared in the 1992 documentary Ayrton Senna: Racing Is In My Blood and also became known as the 'hosepipe' car, thanks to famous photographs of the Brazilian washing it himself.

More than 35 years after it was registered, the NSX sold at RM Sotheby's The London Auction for £871,250.

Lauda’s welcome gift from Ferrari

After signing for Ferrari ahead of the 1974 season, Niki Lauda was given something rather special to drive away from the track, a 1973 Ferrari 365 GT4 2+2 by Pininfarina. Completed at the Maranello factory in December 1973, Lauda became its first owner as his fruitful relationship started with the Scuderia – a partnership that would later bring him two World Championships.

Originally finished in silver – otherwise known as Argento Metallizzato – the Ferrari was initially registered on Italian 'tourist' plates, with Lauda later taking the car home to Austria. But there was a problem – reportedly high import costs meant keeping it in the country was going to prove expensive, and he eventually parted ways with the car in 1975.

From there, Lauda's Ferrari passed through the hands of several Austrian owners and was repainted in its current metallic red during the 1980s. Underneath, though, it retained that same raucous 4.4-litre V12 engine and five-speed manual gearbox that it had during Lauda's ownership.

After spending some time in storage, the car was returned to roadworthy condition in 2025 before appearing at RM Sotheby's Munich auction, where it sold for €201,250.

Ricciardo’s remarkable Valkyrie

After departing Formula 1, Daniel Ricciardo put one of the most striking cars from his private collection up for sale – a pristine 2023 Aston Martin Valkyrie.

Described as “one of the greatest hypercars of recent years”, the Valkyrie was developed jointly by Aston Martin and Red Bull Racing, with Adrian Newey playing a key role. Ricciardo, who was racing for Red Bull when the project began, later commissioned chassis number 089 to his own specification.

“It feels like a race car and it looks like a race car,” said Ricciardo. “I'm not used to having a roof over my head, but that's the only thing that really feels different, otherwise, it's a pretty straight-up race car.”

The car was finished in ‘Badger Blue’ – a neat link to Ricciardo’s ‘Honey Badger’ nickname – and had covered just 160km, having spent much of its life in his private collection.

One of only 150 Valkyrie coupes produced, it was offered by Broad Arrow Auctions at the Zoute Concours Auction, eventually selling for €2.12 million.

Hamilton’s #44 Chassis

Lewis Hamilton has assembled an enviable collection of cars. At Monza, he arrived in a recently recommissioned Ferrari F40 and revealed that technicians had discovered the number 44 stamped on its engine block. But that is not the only supercar linking Hamilton to his racing number.

Hamilton is widely reported to own a 1995 McLaren F1, chassis 044, which sold for $15.62 million at the Bonhams Quail Lodge Auction in 2017. Although Bonhams did not identify the buyer, the car was later linked to Hamilton after he was reportedly seen driving the silver McLaren in California.

The number is only part of the car’s remarkable history. The 37th road-going F1 built, chassis 044 was also the first imported into the United States and the first to be made fully road legal there.

The story of the McLaren F1 began in 1988, when Gordon Murray, Ron Dennis, Mansour Ojjeh and Creighton Brown discussed building the ultimate road car following McLaren’s dominant 15-win Formula 1 season. The result combined a central driving position and naturally aspirated V12 with ground-breaking carbon-fibre construction, helping make it one of the defining performance cars of its generation.

For many young car fans growing up in the 1990s, the McLaren F1 was the ultimate bedroom-wall poster car – and decades later, its appeal has hardly diminished.

Alonso’s car archive

Fernando Alonso certainly boasts an impressive garage, based on the cars he’s recently bought – including a super rare aluminum-bodied Bugatti Veyron – but he’s also cleared out space in his collection having sold several cars at auction over the years.

Back in 2023, the two-time champion opted to sell his Ferrari Enzo, but it wasn’t just any red Ferrari. Alonso previously owned Chassis No. 1 and completed just 4,800km in this 2002 machine. As well as also driving for the Scuderia during his time in F1, this was a big money item at auction and sold for £4,500,000.

He also sold his 2022 McLaren Elva, which was limited to a production of just 149 machines. Car number 114 was a nod to his race number 14, and sold with the promise that Alonso himself would pass the keys over to the successful buyer.

A seat signed by Schumacher

Michael Schumacher’s 1996 Ferrari F355 GTS came up for auction a few years ago, complete with a huge signature from the seven-time World Champion on the back of the driver’s seat.

Having joined Ferrari for the 1996 season, after winning two titles with Benetton, the Scuderia gave their new driver a road car – a F355 GTS. Featuring a ‘Blu Le Mans’ paint job, the service book shows that it was delivered to a Ferrari dealership on 30 April 1996, which would have been days after Schumacher's second place at that season’s European Grand Prix at the Nurburgring.

The F355 changed hands several times before finding its way to a motoring journalist, who later spoke to Schumacher about the car at the 2012 Belgian Grand Prix.

Jenson Button’s paddock scooter

Not every vehicle associated with an F1 World Champion needs heaps of horsepower. Long before Jenson Button claimed the 2009 title, the Briton could be seen navigating the Grand Prix paddock on something rather more modest: a Honda SZX50 moped.

Finished in full BAR-Honda colours, the 50cc machine served as Button’s personal paddock transport during the 2003 and 2004 seasons, before being given away as a competition prize and subsequently sold at the Goodwood Festival of Speed for £2,990.

More than two decades later, Button’s former runaround returned to the auction block with a mere 415 miles on the clock.

Still bearing a few marks from its paddock life, it sold for £5,040 – almost twice the amount it fetched back in 2004.

title: What time is the 2026 Sao Paulo GP and how can I watch it?
excerpt:
The 2026 Formula 1 season heads to Sao Paulo next for the 20th race weekend of the campaign, with Kimi Antonelli set to arrive in Brazil as this year's World Champion.

Third place last weekend in Mexico City was enough for the Italian to become the youngest World Champion in F1 history, but he will look to add to his nine wins from his championship-winning campaign this weekend.

Mercedes can also secure the Constructors' Championship in Brazil, but the likes of Red Bull and Ferrari could still pose a threat for Grand Prix victory after strong performances last weekend in Mexico.

Head to the RACE HUB or scroll down for more on how and when you can watch the action, along with the global start times for each session.

What time is the Sao Paulo Grand Prix?

The weekend will kick off with Free Practice 1 at 1230 local time on Friday, 6 November, followed by Free Practice 2 later that day at 1600.

A final hour of practice will begin at 1130 on Saturday, 7 November, before Qualifying gets underway at 1500. The Grand Prix itself will take place at 1400 on Sunday, 8 November.

Check out the image below to find all the global start times for Sunday’s race.

How can I watch the Sao Paulo Grand Prix?

You can enjoy coverage from every session live on F1 TV Pro (available in selected countries), which brings fans closer to the action via exclusive features like onboard cameras on all 22 of the drivers’ cars, and access to both Pre-Race and Post-Race Shows.

F1 TV Pro can be streamed easily via Apple TV, Chromecast Generation 2 and above, Android TV, Google TV, Amazon Fire TV, and Roku. F1 TV Pro is free of ad breaks and available with commentary in six languages.

Fans can also watch via F1 TV Premium, a premier service that invites fans to step into the heart of the action with the ability to watch races in 4K Ultra HD/HDR on up to six different devices, as well as a personalised Multiview feature available on select devices with 26 different feeds to choose from.

Viewers can watch every F1 Grand Prix, F1 Sprint, Qualifying and practice session live in 4K Ultra HD/HDR at home, with F2, F3, F1 ACADEMY and Porsche Supercup sessions also available to watch live on the platform.

Alternatively, live timing will be available on F1.com and the F1 app across every session during the Grand Prix weekend.

Where is the 2026 Sao Paulo Grand Prix taking place?

The Sao Paulo Grand Prix will take place at the popular Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace, also known as Interlagos, which is a favourite of drivers and fans.

The current iteration of circuit has been used since 1990 and has been on the calendar every year since, apart from 2020 during COVID.

With its high-speed corners, flowing undulations and long main straight, it poses a challenge for drivers and teams, as well as offering several overtaking opportunities, noticeably into Turn 1.

What is the weather forecast in Sao Paulo?

The weekend looks like it will feature rain at various points, with many previous editions of the race taking place on a wet track.

Practice on Friday could feature heavy rain, although mostly in the morning, with Saturday set to feature thunderstorms throughout the day. The race on Sunday is also at risk of rain, although lighter in intensity.

title: Who impressed our Power Rankings judges in Mexico City?
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli rewrote the history books when he was crowned the 2026 World Champion after his third-place finish at the Mexico City Grand Prix. But who else impressed our Power Rankings judges? Check out the latest scores and overall leaderboard below…

How it works

Our five-judge panel assess each driver after every Grand Prix and score them out of 10 according to their performance across the weekend – taking machinery out of the equation

Our experts’ scores are then averaged out to produce a race score – with those scores then tallied up across the season on our overall Power Rankings Leaderboard (at the bottom of the page)

If anyone can deliver under pressure, it's Max Verstappen, and this weekend was no exception. After his "clumsy" incident with Liam Lawson in FP2, the Red Bull racer charged from fifth to second on the opening lap, capitalising on another tense moment between Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc. He subsequently inherited the lead following Leclerc's penalty and went on to confidently control two restarts as Hamilton persistently challenged him, with shades of their 2021 contest flashing all the way to the chequered flag.

Antonelli wasn't the only one breaking records in Mexico City. Hamilton took his 105th pole position, and first for Ferrari, with a stunning lap to deny George Russell by just 0.009s. However, an early scrap with his team mate saw him lose ground to Verstappen, leaving his chances of victory hanging in the balance. Despite piling on the pressure after the final restart, the seven-time champion ultimately had to settle for second, finishing just 0.799s behind the Red Bull.

It may not have been a race win, but Antonelli's improvement from P4 to P3 via a fearless pass on Charles Leclerc gave him the points he needed to seal the Drivers' Championship. His season had already demonstrated just how much he's improved since his rookie campaign, but another mature drive to the podium in Mexico City made him a more than worthy victor in the standings.

With his seat still unconfirmed for 2027, Liam Lawson's mission to prove he deserves a spot on the grid got a boost in Mexico City, albeit only after he was disqualified from Qualifying for a technical breach. Combined with the FP2 contact with Verstappen, it unnecessarily put him on the back foot, but his charge from the pit lane to P7, helped by some post-race penalties for others, was mightily impressive.

Although McLaren flew in final practice to drag themselves into pole contention, it wasn't to be for Lando Norris as he struggled to repeat the "magical" lap that saw him top the Q2 times. He therefore qualified sixth and was hindered by the squad's insufficient pace advantage, which left him stuck behind Russell and Leclerc over two separate stints before finishing fifth.

After a challenging run of races, Arvid Lindblad rediscovered his confidence in Mexico City, reaching Q3 and qualifying ninth as Racing Bulls emerged as the pick of the midfield. The rookie carried that promising pace into Sunday, making a strong start and running comfortably inside the points while managing his tyres. He was battling Oscar Piastri for seventh when contact between the pair sent him into the barriers, bringing a premature end to what had otherwise been an impressive weekend.

While jumping into an F1 car midway through a weekend is a somewhat unique challenge, Ryo Hirakawa took it in his stride and relied on his years of motorsport experience to keep it clean. After being knocked out in Q1, he stayed out of trouble and got stuck into some battles en route to P10, giving Haas their sole point of the round as Ollie Bearman retired with damage.

Sergio Perez's 300th Grand Prix may not have delivered the home result he had hoped for, but the Cadillac driver still gave the Mexican fans plenty to cheer about. After missing FP3 and qualifying towards the back of the grid, Perez made an encouraging start and climbed as high as P13, holding his own against faster machinery. Unfortunately, a slow pit stop and a subsequent penalty for speeding in the pit lane compromised his afternoon, leaving him to finish P16 despite a spirited performance.

Ollie Bearman looked set to add another points finish to his tally in Mexico City before his race came to an abrupt end through no fault of his own. Having recovered from a difficult final practice session to qualify 15th, the Haas driver made an impressive start and worked his way into the points fight. However, after overtaking Nico Hulkenberg at the red flag restart, he was struck from behind by the Audi driver at Turn 4, sustaining damage that forced him into retirement.

Reliability troubles threatened to derail Gabriel Bortoleto's Mexico City weekend, with the Audi driver missing valuable running in practice and heading into Qualifying on the back foot. Despite starting 13th, the Brazilian kept himself in contention during a chaotic race, making the most of the opportunities that came his way to cross the line in P11. A series of post-race penalties subsequently promoted him to eighth, providing a welcome points finish after a challenging weekend for the team.

Missing out

Just missing out on this week's Power Rankings list are Williams' Alex Albon, who finished 12th, and Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, whose hopes of a podium were dashed by a five-second time penalty. Alpine's Franco Colapinto also narrowly missed the cut after another solid performance in Mexico City.

title: Lindblad offers verdict on Piastri collision in Mexico
excerpt:
Arvid Lindblad has stated he and Oscar Piastri "were in a genuine fight" in the closing stages of the Mexico City Grand Prix, with the Racing Bulls driver ultimately crashing out of the race after a collision.

Lindblad had circulated in the points for much of Sunday's 71-lap race at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, with the F1 rookie jumping ahead of Piastri for P7 after a mid-race restart following a red flag.

The pair battled over several laps, with Piastri eventually moving to the outside of Lindblad into Turn 1 on Lap 58, the McLaren driver making contact with the Racing Bulls car ahead.

The contact on the left-rear sent Lindblad into the air and crashing into the wall on the exit of Turn 2, with Piastri handed a 10-second penalty post-race for the incident.

"I don't want to properly comment on it until I've seen all the footage," said Lindblad immediately afterwards.

"But in the end, the pace was good, we were in a genuine fight with him. He was stuck behind me for over 10 laps. I was committed to fighting for that position and I wasn't just going to let him drive around the outside of me easily."

Despite failing to score for the third race in succession, Lindblad was pleased with his general performance over the weekend having lost confidence over the summer following a spate of crashes.

"Being completely honest, I lost a bit my rhythm after Madrid, Baku where I had the two crashes," he said.

"I wasn't just as confident to hustle the car as much and put it on the limit. I think I can kind of do okay in Qualifying but in the race it was showing more and just happy this weekend I felt more like myself.

"I think the race pace was really good, which has been a weakness of mine for the last few races, so just happy to be back in my mojo again and looking forward to Brazil."

Team mate Liam Lawson was able to finish P10 on-the-road having staretd from the pit lane after being disqualified in Qualifying for a technical infringement.

But the New Zealander was promoted up to seventh after Piastri's penalty, plus a further two positions at the expense of Alpine drivers Franco Colapinto and Pierre Gasly.

"It was a tough race. The first part was a big struggle for us, we missed the VSC, didn't box, and then we boxed for our second stop the lap before the Safety Car, so it was just really unlucky and lost a lot of race time," said Lawson.

"Then obviously the red flag helped us, we got a restart from P15 and then I just tried to attack as much as possible. It's a good recovery for us."

title: F1’s youngest World Champions as Antonelli smashes record
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli is champion of the world, and the youngest ever to do it in F1 history. The Italian has rewritten the record books, in what is only his second season in the sport, after his third place finish in Mexico City sealed the deal.

With the 20-year-old now confirmed as the sport's 36th World Champion, F1.com takes a look at the five youngest title winners after Antonelli's record-breaking feat.

5. Max Verstappen

First championship: 2021

Age: 24 years and 73 days

The youngest driver to ever start a Grand Prix at 17 years and 166 days, Max Verstappen also surpassed Sebastian Vettel as F1’s youngest Grand Prix winner in the 2016 Spanish Grand Prix, but amid a period of Mercedes control, he did not quite have the chance to become the sport’s youngest champion.

In 2021, he put an end to the Silver Arrows’ stunning run and quashed Lewis Hamilton’s hopes of taking a record eighth drivers’ title at the Abu Dhabi finale – the first time since 1974 that the protagonists were equal on points heading into the last round.

Verstappen went on to win the 2022, 2023 and 2024 titles in fine style, making him a four-time champion at 27 years old, before narrowly missing out to McLaren’s Lando Norris in 2025.

4. Fernando Alonso

First championship: 2005

Age: 24 years and 57 days

After an impressive rookie season with Minardi in 2001, Fernando Alonso made himself at home at Renault’s works team, who steadily grew into a race-winning and title-contending force as the noughties developed.

New regulations for 2005 provided the perfect platform to take the next step and, after five successive drivers’ titles for Ferrari star Michael Schumacher, the young Spaniard was the man to end that dominant spell.

Alonso backed up his breakthrough title triumph in 2006 (when he became F1’s youngest double champion at the time), scoring 134 points to Schumacher’s 121 in an intense battle that went down to the wire.

Spells at various teams and several championship near misses have followed over the years, meaning he is still chasing that elusive third crown at the age of 45.

3. Lewis Hamilton

First championship: 2008

Age: 23 years and 300 days

After arriving at McLaren for 2007 as a double World Champion, Alonso experienced a fierce rivalry with newcomer Hamilton, who showed no signs of settling for ‘Number 2’ status.

Alonso and Hamilton were closely matched throughout that campaign, and ended it level on points – only to both be pipped by Ferrari rival Kimi Raikkonen at the final round.

While Alonso departed, Hamilton remained, and he found himself in title contention once more in 2008. It all led up to the nail-biting Brazilian Grand Prix, which went down in F1 history when the British youngster passed Toyota’s Timo Glock in the dying laps to become the youngest F1 champion at 23 years and 300 days old.

If he can clinch another title with Ferrari in 2027, he would become the third-oldest F1 champion behind Giuseppe Farina (43 years, 10 months, four days) and Juan Manuel Fangio (46 years, 1 month, 11 days).

2. Sebastian Vettel

First championship: 2010

Age: 23 years and 133 days

Vettel entered the 2010 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix 15 points shy of Alonso, but dramatically emerged as the youngest F1 World Champion.

Incidentally, he became the youngest-ever double (then triple, then quadruple) champion in the following years, as the German and Red Bull enjoyed a period of dominance.

But that is not all. He had already become the youngest-ever F1 points scorer for BMW Sauber at the 2007 United States Grand Prix, and followed that up in 2008 by becoming the then youngest polesitter and race winner at Monza.

1. Kimi Antonelli

First championship: 2026

Age: 20 years and 68 days

Vettel’s pole record was beaten by Kimi Antonelli earlier this year, as the Italian – still a teenager at the time – charged to P1 on the grid for the Chinese Grand Prix, where he also claimed his maiden win (putting him second to Verstappen in the all-time list).

Antonelli has gone from strength to strength since then, emerging as Mercedes’ lead driver in a new era of regulations to pull away from team mate George Russell in the standings and charge towards the title at just 20 years old.

It means he is comfortably the youngest champion in F1 history, eclipsing the legendary names before him in this list, and setting a new record that is unlikely to be beaten anytime soon…

title: Russell shares emotional reflection on 2026 in candid post
excerpt:
George Russell has opened up about the challenges of his 2026 campaign in an emotional social media post, admitting that the season has been one of the toughest of his career following Mercedes team mate Kimi Antonelli's World Championship triumph.

Russell took to Instagram on Monday to reflect on a year that had began with title ambitions but has since been marked by reliability issues and inconsistent performances, with the Briton acknowledging that he has struggled to rediscover his best form.

The post came a day after Antonelli secured his maiden Drivers' Championship at the Mexico City Grand Prix, becoming the youngest World Champion in Formula 1 history after finishing third behind Red Bull’s Max Verstappen and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton.

Russell, meanwhile, endured another frustrating afternoon at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, finishing sixth after a power deployment issue on the opening lap cost him several positions, while a subsequent collision with Isack Hadjar resulted in a 10-second time penalty.

Reflecting on his season, Russell wrote: "Now feels like a pretty suitable moment to speak from the heart.

"This season started off exactly how I had hoped but it very quickly unravelled with tough luck and poor performances. It’s been the first proper season of my career where I’ve had more bad days than good.

"Has it been tough to deal with? Yes, very. Has it been tough to pick myself up week in, week out? Yes, very. Confusion at times? Often. All I know is that I’ve given it my all and 2026 was not meant to be my year."

Russell began the campaign strongly with victory at the season-opening Australian Grand Prix, but his championship challenge gradually faded as Antonelli established himself at the front of the field.

Despite victories in Austria and Azerbaijan, Russell has struggled to consistently extract the maximum performance from Mercedes' W17, with Team Principal Toto Wolff pointing to the car's narrow operating window as a contributing factor. His difficulties continued in Mexico City, where a power deployment issue compromised his race after narrowly missing out on pole position.

Following the Grand Prix, Wolff admitted that Russell was "distraught" about the outcome, praising the Briton for congratulating Antonelli despite his own disappointment.

In his Instagram message, Russell again paid tribute to his team mate, writing: "I want to sincerely congratulate Kimi on what has been an absolutely incredible season. You truly deserve the Championship."

He also acknowledged Mercedes' return to the front of the grid under the new regulations, thanking those involved in developing the championship-winning package.

"Thank you to the team for producing the best car and power unit this season; it’s been inspiring to see everyone coming together over four tough years to bring Mercedes back to the top," he added.

With four rounds remaining in the 2026 campaign, Russell is now looking to finish the season strongly before turning his attention to next year, when he and Antonelli are set to continue as Mercedes team mates.

He continued: "Now, all I can promise is that for the rest of this season, and into the next one, I will be giving my absolute all to rediscover the performance I have been capable of producing for the majority of my career and fingers crossed a little bit of luck returns. Thanks for all the support."

title: Breaking: Haas announce Esteban Ocon replacement for Sao Paulo F1 Grand Prix
excerpt:
Haas has named Rafael Camara as Esteban Ocon's replacement for this weekend's Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

Frenchman Ocon was stood down from driving duties on Saturday morning of the Mexico City Grand Prix, after what is believed to have been a heated exchange after Friday practice with team boss Ayao Komatsu and race engineer Laura Mueller regarding the FP2 run plan.

It has been confirmed that Ocon will not return to the team in 2026, ahead of his planned departure at the end of the season.

The team confirmed that Ocon was not dropped due to ill health, with the one-time grand prix winner taking to social media on Saturday evening to rebut claims of physical violence in the meeting, writing that: "I categorically reject any reports or allegations suggesting that any form of physical violence was used to resolve any differences of any nature.

"I strongly condemn violence in all its forms and firmly believe that disagreements should always be handled with professionalism, respect, and mutual understanding."

He was replaced by Ryo Hirakawa for the weekend, with the Le Mans winner, who had deputised for Ocon in FP1 for his second mandatory rookie slot, taking over, and after multiple penalties, banked a point on his debut in 10th place - the 82nd driver to do so in F1 world championship history.

However, Hirakawa is not available this weekend in Sao Paulo, as the race clashes with the World Endurance Championship season finale - the Monza Six Hours in Italy.

The #8 Toyota crew of Hirakawa, Sebastien Buemi, and Brendon Hartley are on the cusp of winning the drivers' title, with a 17-point lead over the #7 Toyota with 26 points up for grabs.

Should Hirakawa not race in the WEC, and Buemi and Hartley double-crew, they would be the official 2026 drivers' champions if they did win the title, and Hirakawa would not be able to join his crew-mates in being called a 2026 WEC world champion.

This means Haas was faced with a choice of trying to get its 2027 driver Camara in the car ahead of time to make his debut, or go with its reserve driver Jack Doohan, whose performance in the TPC tests seriously impressed Haas and made him a contender for Ocon's 2027 seat, which ultimately went to Camara.

Haas has been able to agree an early release from Ferrari for Camara, who will become the team's fourth driver of the season - the maximum which is allowed in the rules.

For the rest of the season, Haas must now field a driver line-up consisting of two from incumbent Oliver Bearman, Camara and Hirakawa.

There was no confirmation from the team on who will drive the second car alongside Bearman for the remainder of the season after the Sao Paulo GP weekend.

[Article continues below]

Haas statement in full

In a statement, Haas also confirmed that Ocon would not be returning to the team, bringing to a close his F1 career, for now.

"We have now notified Esteban Ocon that he will not return to a race seat with Haas F1 Team this season," it began.

"Such decisions are never made lightly, as was the case in Mexico City - but then, as now, we feel this is firmly in the best interest of the team moving forward.

"The conversations that ultimately unfolded between the team and Esteban remain an internal matter, and we will continue to respect the private nature of closed-door situations.

"Looking ahead, we've chosen Rafael Camara to drive alongside Ollie Bearman at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix. Having excelled in his TPC outing in August, we know Rafa's capabilities, and we're looking forward to welcoming him into the team this weekend and working with him through his Formula 1 debut driving the VF-26 in Brazil."

title: Cadillac encouraged to pursue Liam Lawson: 'That's suddenly looking very strong'
excerpt:
Karun Chandhok has implored Cadillac to explore signing Liam Lawson, whose F1 future remains uncertain with Racing Bulls yet to finalise its 2027 driver lineup.

Lawson has been in exceptional form this season, and the paddock consensus is that the New Zealander has done more than enough to secure his future within the Red Bull family.

However, the situation is far from simple, and despite being comfortably best of the rest in the F1 drivers' standings, Lawson could lose his seat to F2 title challenger and highly-touted Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov.

The Faenza-based squad has yet to announce either of its choices for next year, but Arvid Lindblad, who is having an impressive rookie campaign, is broadly expected to keep his drive, meaning the other seat is a straight fight between Lawson and Tsolov.

But with Valtteri Bottas' future at Cadillac also appearing less than secure and heir apparent Colton Herta disappointing in F2, Lawson has come in frame for the seat alongside Sergio Perez, something Chandhok would happily see.

"We're hearing more and more that Liam Lawson's seat is under threat," the former F1 driver said to Sky Sports F1. "I think that's one of the most unjust things I've heard this season.

"If he's on the market... if you're Cadillac and Liam Lawson's a free agent, do you take him over Colton Herta?

"I know there's commercial reasons and marketing reasons to have an American driver, but actually, suddenly, if you're looking at a Lawson-Perez lineup, that's suddenly looking very strong, isn't it?

"So, I don't know. I think there seems to be a lot more at play. Two months ago, it felt like the driver market had settled, and now there are a few more balls in play."

[Article continues below]

Wider advantages to signing Lawson

Standing ninth in the championship, Lawson has scored 83 points over the first 19 rounds of the season, including 14 in his three-race cameo for Red Bull.

That is more than the next two drivers, Pierre Gasly and Lindblad, combined.

Not only that, but Bernie Collins sees wider advantages to Cadillac opting for the New Zealander than what he has achieved on circuit this year.

"I totally agree with what Karun was saying there; Liam Lawson, he's done a very impressive job with Racing Bulls this year — he scored the majority of the points that they have on the board, double his team-mate," Collins said.

"He's been very consistent throughout the year; he's doing really, really well there. He did well when he stepped into the Red Bull; he was a bit unlucky in one of the races [the Italian Grand Prix].

"However, look at the advantage for Cadillac of taking someone like him. He has run [in] that RB, so he knows a lot about that car. That car is performing very well. He knows their engine. He's also stepped in the Red Bull, so he takes a lot of data from that as well.

"So he comes with a lot of good information, if you're able to take him, on a car that really needs the development."

title: Fernando Alonso issues 'cannot survive' claim as Barcelona secures major coup
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso believes Spanish motorsport "cannot survive" without top-level racing in Barcelona, after a deal was announced with IndyCar.

For the first time, IndyCar, in its current guise, is to race in Europe from 2027 with a deal agreed after the success of five-time series champion Alex Palou.

The news comes after the Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya formally enters a bi-annual rotation on the F1 calendar, with the venue not on the 2027 calendar - the first time it has not been since it hosted its first race in 1991.

It will return on rotation with the Belgian Grand Prix in 2029, with Spa taking the even-numbered years until the end of the arrangement after the 2032 season.

Reflecting on the news, Alonso felt that Barcelona, which lost the formal Spanish Grand Prix to the new Madring street circuit in the Spanish capital, was a crucial part in inspiring the next generation of Spanish racers.

"I think it's going to be good, and it is an historic event for our country, and Barcelona does have the benefit of having a permanent circuit," Alonso told media, including RacingNews365.

"You know that you have the opportunity to test any day of the year, but also to host races here and there. They did the WEC, and now Indy, and they do MotoGP, so that's why, when we compare street circuits to the normal conventional circuits, that's the biggest advantage.

"Barcelona is crucial for motorsport in Spain. We cannot survive without Barcelona for the younger categories, for the people from go-karts that they go testing the F4 for the first time, and FRECA, Formula 3 and even Moto3.

"You have to have a circuit that you can go there, and with IndyCar, this is another example of how good and how lucky we are."

[Article continues below]

Future IndyCar expansion

Despite the news, Alonso did not believe that wider expansion into the markets outside the United States was something IndyCar would do bar one or two events.

"IndyCar is very specific to the US market, and one of the things that is more penalising in F1 for the drivers and for the teams, is that the cost goes very high when you travel around the world," he said.

"So it has some benefits and some downside. I think they need to keep it somehow in the US, and have one or two one-off races, but I don't think that they will keep going elsewhere."

title: The Andretti Formula E secret weapon with 'world champion' target
excerpt:
Andretti's new Formula E development driver Callum Voisin has ambitions of becoming a "world champion" and is very much a rising star who, it turns out, is not so new to the American outfit after all.

Voisin was announced last week as Andretti's development driver for the start of the Gen4 era, but in actual fact, he continued working for the team after representing it in the Madrid rookie test in March earlier this year.

It was the Briton's second Formula E rookie test, having represented Cupra Kiro the year prior in Berlin. In both tests, Voisin was hugely impressive, going 10th quickest in the Spanish capital. His performance left Andretti eager to keep him on.

A month after the test, Voisin started supporting Andretti's pre-event set-up on the simulator, around the time the team's results on circuit suddenly improved.

Voisin's pre-event simulator support for Jake Dennis and Felipe Drugovich coincided with Andretti's strongest run of the season, with the team scoring 113 points across Sanya, Shanghai and Tokyo.

While he has spent most of 2026 with Andretti, the 20-year-old was unsure exactly where he stood with the squad heading into the upcoming season and the Gen4 era, with last week's announcement coming as a pleasant surprise.

Asked how soon he returned to work for Andretti after the Jarama rookie test, Voisin revealed during an interview with RacingNews365: "It was pretty soon after. I'd say, I don't know, a month. Yeah, we got some stuff sorted pretty quickly, and then it was just doing the kind of pre-event set-up.

"So, yeah, that was about it. But, yeah, it all happened fairly quickly, and then I was pretty instantly integrated into the team. But obviously, it was always a bit... I didn't 100% know in what capacity I was in the team.

"I knew that I was doing the pre-event stuff and helping Jake and Felipe out on the DIL, but at the same time, I didn't know if it was a permanent role or if it was kind of just for the rest of the season.

"I didn't really know, so for me, it was a nice surprise to get kind of that [confirmation]."

Article continues below...

Callum Voisin expects 'insane' Gen4 to raise physical demands

It has been a strong year for the young star, who, alongside supporting Andretti, raced in the Porsche Carrera Cup GB, where he sealed the 2026 title with Rosland Gold by Century Motorsport with two races to spare, finishing the campaign with nine victories.

Moving from single-seaters to GT racing after leaving Formula 3 has so far worked well for Voisin, who has kept himself firmly in the Formula E shop window. He aims to continue with a GT programme in 2027.

RacingNews365 understands Voisin will take on rookie free practice duties and a rookie test spot for Andretti in Miami next year, giving him further track time as he edges closer to a potential full-time seat.

Moving from the Gen3 Evo to the Gen4 is a huge step up for Voisin, who is hungry and excited for the challenge ahead, resulting in regular messages to team principal Campbell Hobson.

Looking ahead to working on a car as advanced as the Gen4, Voisin said: "I'm so excited. I keep messaging Campbell [Hobson], asking when the simulator is ready to get going. Because, yeah, for me, I mean, the numbers look pretty insane.

"I haven't managed to see much footage, but from what I have seen, it looks amazing, and I think it's a real challenge for everyone. To be honest, I think Formula E has been growing at a rapid rate, more than any other motorsport series, I would say.

"But for me, this is a huge jump, and certainly physically as well. I think the drivers are really going to have to step it up in terms of the training that they do, which for me is always exciting. If a car really demands a lot from the body, I think it's always a bit more rewarding when you get it right, I guess, and it shows the people you work the hardest."

Pressed on whether he harbours genuine ambitions of a full-time Formula E race seat, Voisin left little doubt about where his motorsport future is aimed.

Discussing whether he holds a serious interest in a future Formula E race seat, Voisin explained: "Yeah, absolutely. I think I've said in pretty much every interview that I've done, my goal in motorsport is to become a world champion, and Formula E is one of those championships that ticks that box.

"So for me, it's definitely a future that I see myself in. Obviously, Formula E is a difficult championship to get into. There's no proper, I would say, there's no support series, no proper ladder system in a way. So it's not the easiest for a driver to get in. But, you know, it rewards a driver for being very adaptable."

title: McLaren make fresh upgrade decision as Red Bull gain sudden F1 upper-hand
excerpt:
McLaren is to unveil a raft of fresh upgrades in the Sao Paulo Grand Prix as it looks to wrestle back third in the constructors' from Red Bull.

Max Verstappen's victory in Mexico City, coupled with Isack Hadjar's ninth-place finish, allowed Red Bull to leap into third place in the constructors' on 382 points to McLaren on 365 - who only scored through Lando Norris's fifth place after Oscar Piastri lost his seventh due to a 10-second time penalty for colliding with Arvid Lindblad.

Red Bull has won three of the previous four grands prix, just as McLaren's MCL40 has dipped in competitiveness, with the winners of the last four constructors' titles now in a fight behind Mercedes and Ferrari for the bronze-medal position.

In a bid to regain the upper hand, the car will be boosted with a fresh raft of upgrades this weekend in Brazil.

The front and rear wings are going to be upgraded, with "small floor components" also set to be brought. McLaren says "the aim is to unlock further aerodynamic performance and refine the car’s balance, supporting the ongoing push to strengthen competitiveness."

Reflecting on the upgrades, chief technical officer, aerodynamics, Peter Prodromou spoke of the hope of regaining some momentum - and also having one eye on the 2027 MCL41 machine.

"We’ve got some updates coming to the car across the front wing, rear wing and some floor components as part of our normal development cycle," he began.

"The aim is to make up ground, improve our performance over the remaining races and build momentum into next year.

"São Paulo has been a good circuit for us in the past and is a fairly representative track, so we’re hopeful these upgrades can help us take another step towards the front.

"The season isn't over yet: these upgrades are designed to improve the car now and help us in our fight for third in the championship.

"While the learning we take from these upgrades will feed into next year’s development, we also expect to carry over the concept of the new front wing into the launch specification of next year’s car."

title: How Donald Trump and a dead cat will finally answer F1's Qatar and Abu Dhabi question
excerpt:
First things first, the dead cat referenced in the headline of this article is only metaphorical, and Tiddles remains unharmed.

On Tuesday, November 3rd, the United States is holding its midterm elections, and the results will be crucial for president Donald Trump's reaction and whether the crisis in the Middle East spikes again, which will have an impact on F1's Qatar and Abu Dhabi Grands Prix.

Pencilled in for November 30th and December 6th, the current state of play for F1 is that the races will be going ahead as planned, although Imola is being prepared as a back-up for Abu Dhabi's slot should both races fall through.

F1's decision will be centred around the official travel advice from the United Kingdom Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), which currently states, at the time of writing, that: "British nationals in, or planning to travel through, the Middle East should be prepared for possible flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions." It does not advise against travel - a status which, if issued should tensions re-escalate in the next week, would almost certainly see the plug pulled.

But that advice will be decided upon after the reaction to the midterms of the occupant of the egg-shaped office in the West Wing of 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue.

[Article continues below]

© XPBimages

What are the midterms?

In the United States, congressional elections are held every two years, with the presidential election every four.

With Trump defeating Kamala Harris in 2024, the White House is not on the ballot again until 2028, meaning the 2026 elections focus exclusively on electing the new Congress - that is the Senate and the House.

Senators serve six-year terms, meaning one-third of the 100-member body are facing voters on Tuesday, with all 435 members of the House up for a new two-year term.

Although the sitting president is never on the ballot in the midterms, by their very nature, coming midway through a four-year presidential term, they are seen as a referendum on the president's performance in office during the first two years of the term.

For example, during the 2018 midterms, in Trump's first term, the House flipped from Republican control to Democratic. In Barack Obama's first midterms in 2010, a strong Democratic majority was wiped out in favour of a Republican wave.

On paper, Tuesday's elections are proving to be a challenge for Trump. As the cost of living soars and energy and fuel prices spike after his decision to attack Iran earlier this year, the voting public is growing wary and tired of the economic situation - especially as the war drags on.

It is expected that the House will flip to the Democrats in Tuesday's vote, with the Senate harder to flip. There are also gubernatorial races in 36 of the 50 states, with the state governors proving loyal foot soldiers for the sitting president and his agenda.

A Democratic house will prove problematic for Trump - as it can launch investigations, demand documents, and stall his legislative programme - something no sitting president wants.

And here's where our dead cat comes in - namely the Middle East.

[Article continues below]

© XPBimages

F1's Middle East question

After the war broke out earlier this year after the United States and Israel launched attacks on the Iranian regime, F1 tyre testing in Bahrain was cancelled, and the Bahrain and Saudi Arabian GPs, set for April, were postponed - not officially cancelled.

Bahrain was eventually held in Malaysia in October, with the only casualty so far being the Jeddah race, with Qatar and Abu Dhabi set to go ahead as planned.

However, should the midterms go badly for Trump, a very tempting option is to throw a dead cat across the table and distract attention away from his domestic woes and attack Iran - something Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, as per a report in the Financial Times, is urging the American president to do as he fights for his own political survival after his coalition failed to achieve a majority in last week's elections there.

The picture will be clearer later in the week once the midterm results have been declared. Trump has indicated that he will not attack Iran with talks underway about a ceasefire, but this must be taken with a pinch of salt given this president's unpredictability.

For F1, the end of the road it is currently kicking the can down is approaching, with it and the FIA keeping a close eye on the developments, with assessments being made constantly about whether it is safe to race in the Middle East.

For MotoGP, its crunch point is coming this very weekend with the Qatar Grand Prix. Reports from Malaysia last weekend indicated that 19 riders did not want to race, and one report claiming that teams and riders had been threatened with a ban from the final two rounds if they did not travel to Lusail.

The Yahama factory team has withdrawn from the event.

[Article continues below]

© XPB Images

A view from a team

After the Mexico City Grand Prix, Audi racing director Allan McNish addressed the situation regarding the Qatar and Abu Dhabi races.

"We're going to Qatar and Abu Dhabi," he told media, including RacingNews365.

"All the travel, logistics, everything is going in that direction. Obviously, we're waiting to see if there is any change, and if there is, we will react to it, but at the moment, it is status quo.

"I don't see why we would be put at an incorrect risk. From my perspective, if all the due diligence is done, and I would expect all the due diligence is being done, then we're taking the circus there.

"It's not just one or two teams; it's a big circus. So, I think [F1 and the FIA] would be doing their background homework. But it is a situation that I think we're all very aware of, and we're all very aware that it is a moving target."

So far, F1 has been able to avoid making a decision by making the decision to delay the decision, but decision time is approaching - and for the first time, all the pieces will be on the chessboard to see the state of play - but the delicately constructed game might just be disrupted when the dead cat lands slap bang in the middle of the board...

title: Why Kimi Antonelli did not receive his champion's trophy despite winning F1 title
excerpt:
There was one glaring admission from Kimi Antonelli's title celebrations on Sunday as he became the youngest F1 champion: his trophy.

The Italian had received his standard third-place trophy for finishing behind Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton, but the big trophy was not awarded - and was only seen on a big TV screen behind him, with his signature digitally added to the 35 drivers who had conquered the world before him - two of whom hoisted him aloft on their shoulders.

When victorious moments in sport are memorised, normally the iconic photo is of the team captain or individual picking up their trophy.

Think of England captain Bobby Moore holding the Jules Rimet Trophy after England won the 1966 FIFA World Cup. Think Michael Jordan hugging the NBA trophy after the Chicago Bulls won the 1991 championship. Think even of a sport where the most iconic trophy of all isn't even a trophy: the Green Jacket at Augusta for winning The Masters - but the new F1 world champion does not get this opportunity.

Sometimes, the new champion is not even on the podium, and despite being picked up for an interview by the commercial rights holder, won't take their place among the top three unless they finished in it.

Instead, Antonelli will receive his trophy, not in the full glare of the public, but at a black-tie gala in Shanghai in December.

The reason the F1 world champion does not receive their championship trophy instantly is that it is the centrepiece award at the FIA annual prize-giving ceremony, this year being held in China.

There, the world champions from every FIA-sanctioned championship, from F1 to the WEC, the WRC, and karting, will gather in one place, with the FIA keen not to award the F1 championship trophy, as it is believed that having the F1 world champion in the same place as a karting champion sends a good message to those just starting out.

Although the commercial rights holder (Liberty Media) controls the commercial side of F1, it is the FIA that retains the sporting and regulatory authority. Therefore, as Antonelli was crowned FIA Formula 1 world champion - it is the FIA whose authority the matter is covered by.

Moves have been made in the past to try and relax the situation - but given the prospect of technical challenges and potential disqualifications, the FIA is reluctant to hand over a trophy to a driver and then potentially be forced to take it away again.

Therefore, Antonelli, although world champion, will not be officially so until he is crowned on December 12th - at which point Lando Norris ceases to be the reigning world champion as he hands back the trophy, which is then Antonelli's for the year, at least.

title: Fewest races before becoming F1 champion after Kimi Antonelli success
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has become the youngest-ever F1 world champion, in just his second season of grand prix racing.

The Italian's third place finish in the Mexico City Grand Prix was enough to secure him the crown, as he smashed Sebastian Vettel's old record from 2010 of 23 years, 4 months, 11 days.

On Sunday, November 1st, Antonelli was 20 years, 2 months, 7 days old, beating Vettel by 3 years, 2 months, 4 days.

Antonelli is the first Italian since Alberto Ascari in 1953 to be crowned champion - and third overall after the very first title winner, Giuseppe Farina in 1950 and the first of Ascari's two titles in 1952.

He is the 36th driver to be crowned F1 champion - and just the fifth driver to win their first title in their first or second season.

The others are Juan Manuel Fangio (1951), Jacques Villeneuve (1997), and Lewis Hamilton (2008), whilst Farina is the only champion to win in their first season, although this must be caveated with the fact that it was the first year of the world championship, so someone had to win...

In terms of number of races started, if the unique circumstances of Farina's title win are excepted, it is Fangio who has waited the fewest number of grands prix before being world champion - taking 13 starts to be crowned champion at the end of his second season of 1951.

At the other end of the scale, Nico Rosberg's sole title came after 206 races in 2016, in his 11th season, whilst Nigel Mansell has had the longest career in terms of seasons, finally winning the title in 1992 in his 13th season.

As for Antonelli, he took the title in his 43rd grand prix, which places him 13th on the list in terms of the fewest number of races taken.

Between them, the 36 champions have taken 2.457 races combined to win their first title, with an average of 68.3 - with 1996 champion Damon Hill the closest to this on 67 starts.

The table below records Jochen Rindt's figure as 60 races started. Rindt was killed in practice for the 1970 Italian Grand Prix, ahead of what would have been his 61st start. The number is recorded as the number of starts he made, with the late Austrian being assured of the title later in the year after Jacky Ickx failed to overtake his tally of 45 points.

To this day, Rindt remains the only posthumous world champion.

title: Fred Vasseur told to act before Ferrari situation 'gets really bad'
excerpt:
Nico Rosberg has implored Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur to "act" and implement clear racing guidelines for Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc to adhere to.

The words of warning from the 2016 F1 drivers' champion come after Hamilton and Leclerc clashed on the first lap of the Mexico City Grand Prix.

Not for the first time this season, the Ferrari team-mates racing each other have cost Scuderia points. And at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, the pair squandered the ideal position from which to fight for victory, having emerged from the opening sequence of corners in first and second.

Vasseur was keen to express how unacceptable he viewed the incident, citing what he believed to be a "lack of respect" for all those who work for and represent the Italian team.

Hamilton was equally unimpressed by Leclerc's aggressive antics, venting his frustration over team radio during the race and sharing pointed remarks after the chequered flag, having finished second with his team-mate down in fourth.

To Rosberg, however, it is on the Ferrari boss to rein that behaviour in by establishing rules of engagement for his two drivers.

"It's really Fred Vasseur; he needs to start to act," he told Sky Sports F1. "Because, as Lewis said, before the race, there was no discussion — like clear racing guidelines between the two, and it needs to happen.

"Otherwise, it's just going to keep going like this, and it gets really bad when the drivers take it in their own hands and disregard whatever's being discussed and just take it in their own hands and sort it out on track and barge the other guy out of the way.

"That can very quickly happen, and it's already kind of happening."

Rosberg: Leclerc had already 'messed up'

The main point of contention came at Turn 4, when Leclerc swept around the outside of Hamilton. Both approached the corner too quickly and went off-track, with the former cutting across the grass and the latter losing momentum.

The Monegasque driver had planned to give the position back, but Max Verstappen seized upon the opportunity, taking second from the seven-time F1 drivers' champion.

It left Leclerc with no option but to suffer a five-second time penalty, which helped the Red Bull driver take the lead during the pit stop phase.

But Rosberg felt the wheel-to-wheel action had already gone too far, highlighting the out-of-control way in which Leclerc approached the corners prior.

"Even on that first wheel-to-wheel that they had in Turns 2 and 3, Charles was bouncing over the inside into Lewis," he added.

"He was not holding the line, Charles. So already that was too much from Charles, so he messed up already there."

title: Remarkable George Russell statistic highlights extreme misfortune and underperformance
excerpt:
George Russell has endured a bruising F1 season. Coming into the campaign, he was widely expected to clinch his first drivers' championship.

Russell was the bookmakers' favourite; it was anticipated that his Mercedes would be the best car, and he handily beat Kimi Antonelli over the Italian's rookie year in Formula 1.

The Toto Wolff-led team did indeed produce the strongest package, but the title went to his team-mate with four — maybe three — rounds to spare. Not only was it not close, but Russell has slumped to fourth in the standings, in a season that started so well, with an emphatic victory in Melbourne.

Through 19 rounds, Antonelli has amassed a now-insurmountable 380 points, 119 clear of Max Verstappen in second and 130 ahead of Russell.

Not only is the Briton at risk of being surpassed by Charles Leclerc, who is a further five points back, but staggeringly, he has scored fewer points than at this stage of the season last year.

At that point, Russell — who was one of the campaign's standout performers, to the extent Mercedes had to depart from its desire to only hand out one-year contract extensions — sat on 252 points, two more than he has now.

Given how much stronger the W17 is, in terms of pace, than its predecessor, it underlines the bad luck and inconsistency that has characterised the eight-time grand prix winner's year.

Though dominant through the season's opening phase, the Mercedes proved unreliable, and Russell was often on the receiving end of it.

There were smaller issues that cost positions and points, like in China and Japan. And larger power unit failures, like the one seen in Montreal — something that also struck more recently, as was the case at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

There was also further bad luck in Monaco, when the incorrect pit lane speeding penalty snowballed into a pointless round that had looked set to be another podium finish, and his first lap retirement at Spa-Francorchamps, when he collided with former team-mate Lewis Hamilton

But there have also been weekends in which Antonelli has simply outclassed him or Russell has made mistakes, like in the Singapore sprint.

The most pronounced of which might be the Italian Grand Prix. At Monza, Russell started second to Pierre Gasly. His team-mate, in front of his home crowd, came through from P19, albeit with a new power unit, to win.

Either way, 2026 has not been the season Russell would have wanted, nor would he have expected. And that is well illustrated by having two fewer points than at the same stage last year.

title: FIA president makes Kimi Antonelli request in touching tribute to F1 champion
excerpt:
FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has asked Kimi Antonelli to "never change" in a social media congratulation to the new F1 drivers' champion.

Ben Sulayem, who has been at the helm of the motorsports governing body since 2021, shared how "emotional" he is over the Mercedes driver clinching the title in last weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix.

In doing so, Antonelli has become the F1's youngest champion and Italy's first title-winner in 73 years.

The 20-year-old joined Jacques Villeneuve and Lewis Hamilton as the only three drivers to win the crown in just their second season, excluding Juan Manuel Fangio, who took his maiden title in the championship's second campaign, in 1951.

"I am emotional. Congratulations, Kimi," Ben Sulayem said in a social media post from the FIA. "One thing I saw in you, is you work under not just pressure, stress. You never complain.

"I'll just say to you, from the bottom of my heart, congratulations. It's a phenomenon."

The FIA president requested that Antonelli, who is a popular champion, stay who he is now, and not let his success change him.

"But in the meanwhile, I'll just ask you for something: Never change. Keep this Kimi," he added.

"The Kimi I signed the first super licence for him last year, and Kimi as he is now. Just make sure you keep the same Kimi.

"Really, I'm not the only one who's happy. A lot of people are happy. Thank you for making it happen. All the best to you, your family, and your team."

title: WRC champion returns after health issues derail single-seater dream
excerpt:
Two-time World Rally Champion Kalle Rovanperä will return to the WRC with GAZOO Racing TOYOTA in 2027 after health problems derailed his ambition of reaching Formula 1 through single-seater racing.

The 26-year-old left rallying at the end of 2025 to pursue a career in circuit racing, with plans to contest Japan's Super Formula championship in 2026 before progressing to Formula 2 in 2027.

However, the Finn's preparations were disrupted by benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), an inner-ear condition causing dizziness and affecting balance and vision.

The condition forced him to abandon a Super Formula test at Suzuka in December 2025, before further illness interrupted his Formula Regional Oceania Trophy campaign.

Despite returning to Super Formula testing, Rovanperä withdrew from the championship in March following medical evaluations, having struggled with the physical demands of single-seater machinery.

He subsequently focused on his recovery before being cleared to resume driving, with Toyota offering him the opportunity to test its new-generation WRC car.

"I'm really happy to have the opportunity to compete in rallies with GAZOO Racing TOYOTA again next year. This team has always felt like family to me, and in a way I never really felt that I had left.

I'm enjoying having the chance to do some different things, but rallying has been a huge part of my life, and I naturally started to miss the driving after a while," said Rovanperä.

Rovanperä will reunite with co-driver Jonne Halttunen at GAZOO Racing TOYOTA, alongside returning 2019 champion Ott Tänak and Takamoto Katsuta.

Toyota will field two equal, competing teams under the new WRC regulations, with reigning champion Elfyn Evans joining Oliver Solberg and Sami Pajari at TOYOTA RACING.

The manufacturer enters 2027 following six consecutive manufacturers' titles, while Rovanperä returns seeking further success after winning the drivers' championships in 2022 and 2023.

"The main priority this year became my health once I was fit to drive again, the team offered me the opportunity to test the development car, and from there we started making plans for next season," Rovanperä added.

"It's an interesting time to come back, and while the new cars will be very different from what we had before, that makes it an exciting new challenge for me.

"The main thing will be to enjoy the driving and the competition, learn about the car, and see what we can do together."
